title: California voters translate affordability pressure into electoral judgment while trust in government remains thin
source_unit: Public Policy Institute of California, PPIC Statewide Survey: Californians and Their Government, September 2026
geography: California adults and likely voters surveyed September 4-10, 2026

denominator.unit: California adult residents surveyed; likely-voter subgroup used for election questions

affordability_importance.unit: percent of likely voters saying gubernatorial candidates' affordability positions are very important to their vote

somewhat_important.unit: percent of likely voters saying affordability positions are somewhat important

cross_party.value: 69% of Democrats, 65% of Republicans, and 59% of independents call affordability positions very important

political_route.value: cost-of-living judgment is a cross-party electoral filter even amid strong partisan candidate preferences

observations.method: PPIC statewide survey conducted by Ipsos through the probability-based KnowledgePanel in English and Spanish.
observations.uncertainty: Electoral preference and issue importance are stated intentions before the election and do not establish which policy or economic change caused a vote.
observations.subgroup: Likely voters by party, income, region, homeownership, age, gender, and household children.
observations.counterinterpretation: Affordability salience may reflect general economic anxiety rather than a specific assessment of candidates' proposed policies.

price_hardship.unit: percent saying recent price increases caused financial hardship in their household: 21% serious and 37% not serious

housing_strain.unit: percent saying housing costs place a lot or a little financial strain on their family: 24% a lot and 20% a little

income_gradient.value: housing strain falls from 67% below $40,000 income to 57% at $40,000-$99,999 and 32% at $100,000 or more

household_route.value: cost pressure is distributed through both current prices and housing exposure, with a strong income gradient

observations.method: PPIC survey questions on recent price hardship and housing-cost financial strain.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported financial perceptions and do not measure budgets, expenditure records, rent arrears, or causal effects of inflation.
observations.subgroup: Adults by income, race and ethnicity, party, region, renters and homeowners, and households with children.
observations.counterinterpretation: Perceived hardship can be shaped by expectations and local price visibility as well as by realized income loss or spending changes.

observations.period: September 2026; direction, economic expectations, and government trust

state_wrong_direction.unit: percent of adults saying California is headed in the wrong direction

bad_state_economy.unit: percent of adults expecting bad financial times for California in the next 12 months

limited_state_trust.unit: percent saying state government in Sacramento can be trusted to do what is right only some of the time

legitimacy_route.value: economic pessimism and perceived government underperformance reinforce one another as a state-legitimacy signal

observations.method: PPIC statewide survey with repeated time-trend comparisons for direction, economic expectations, and trust.
observations.uncertainty: Direction and trust measures are broad evaluations; they do not identify which public-service experience or policy produced the judgment.
observations.subgroup: Adults and likely voters by party, region, income, race and ethnicity, and education.
observations.counterinterpretation: Negative evaluations can coexist with support for particular programs, ballot measures, or local institutions.

healthcare_dissatisfaction.unit: percent very or somewhat dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care in the country

federal_responsibility.value: about seven in ten say the federal government is responsible for ensuring access to health care

party_split.value: nine in ten Democrats and seven in ten independents assign responsibility to the federal government, while seven in ten Republicans assign responsibility to individuals

public_system_route.value: shared affordability concern can coexist with sharply different views of who owes the remedy

observations.method: PPIC survey questions on affordable health care and responsibility for access.
observations.uncertainty: Responsibility judgments do not measure actual coverage, care access, health outcomes, or support for a specific financing design.
observations.subgroup: Adults by party, income, region, race and ethnicity, and health-care attitudes.
observations.counterinterpretation: A public role can be supported in principle while disagreement remains over federalism, eligibility, financing, or delivery.

related_sources.claim: PPIC prior survey provides time-trend context for affordability and public judgment.
ONS public-opinion evidence provides a complementary cross-national cost, climate, and public-services comparison.

boundary: This record adds a California state-level route from affordability, housing, health-care access, and economic expectations through electoral judgment and trust in government. It uses aggregate survey findings, not respondent-level data, causal policy effects, a forecast of election outcomes, or a universal U.S. estimate.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official PPIC publication page was reviewed for field dates, sample, affordability importance, price hardship, housing strain, state and federal trust, economic expectations, health-care affordability, subgroup patterns, and methods.
